title: What a startup does to you: the founder crucible, and why it's worth it
summary: Jason Cohen reflects on his daughter's birth and colic to argue that a startup, like a child, is a crucible that pushes you past your limits. Reading about the founder roller coaster doesn't prepare you; living it changes you permanently, even if the company fails. A personal essay with little tactical content.

principles.text: A startup is a crucible that doesn't probe your limits, it repeatedly blows past them. Expect that, and it's still worth doing.
principles.quote: A startup is a crucible -- a fiery place that tests your limits, not by probing them but by violently exceeding them, all of the time. It's worth it.

principles.text: You can't learn the founder experience from tweets and books; you only understand it by living it.
principles.quote: You've read the words, now you see that they're only words. Words that don't help much, not really.

principles.text: Even a failed startup leaves you stronger, wiser, and unable to go back to being a cog.
principles.quote: if you do it, even if you "fail," you will come out stronger than you could have ever been without it.

principles.text: Founders who tried and failed rarely regret it; they'd do it again.
principles.quote: I've never met a person who tried a startup, failed, and said they wouldn't have done it all over again.

principles.text: Unlike a child, a startup rarely survives on its own; founders' actions often cause its death.
principles.quote: a startup usually dies regardless of and often due to the actions of the founders
